# Qualifications for Inspection Authorization (IA) With Respect to Major Alterations

**Governing law:** 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart D (Mechanics), §§ 65.91 and 65.95; 14 CFR Part 43 (Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, Rebuilding, and Alteration).
**Interpretation applied:** "inspection auth" = Inspection Authorization issued under Part 65 Subpart D. Aircraft assumed US-registered civil aircraft operated under Part 91 (general case).
**Source currency:** eCFR "current" pages and GovInfo CFR 2025 edition PDFs, fetched 2026-11-15T19:12Z; FAA *Inspection Authorization Information Guide* (secondary).

---

## 1. Short answer

There are **two gates**, and both must be satisfied:

**Gate A — You must hold an Inspection Authorization.** Eligibility is fixed by **§ 65.91(c)**, which contains **five** requirements (listed in § 2 below).

**Gate B — Holding the IA is necessary but not sufficient.** The privilege itself is conditional, per **§ 65.95(a)(1)**: the holder may inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained under a continuous airworthiness program under Part 121) **after a major repair or major alteration**, in accordance with Part 43, **only if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**.

**The negative that answers most real-world questions:** a mechanic certificate (A&P) **without** an IA does not carry this authority. The mechanic certificate qualifies a person to perform and to approve for return to service the work *that mechanic performed*, but approval after a major repair or major alteration is an IA function (or that of another authorization holder under Part 43). The IA also cannot *create* the approved technical data — the IA verifies that the alteration was done per data the FAA has already approved.

---

## 2. Gate A — Eligibility requirements, § 65.91(c)

Verbatim operative text (eCFR current, fetched 2026-11-15):

> (c) To be eligible for an inspection authorization, an applicant must—
> (1) Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each of which is currently effective and has been in effect for a total of at least 3 years;
> (2) Have been actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before the date he applies, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with this chapter;
> (3) Have a fixed base of operations at which he may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week but it need not be the place where he will exercise his inspection authority;
> (4) Have available to him the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance; and
> (5) Pass a written test on his ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and annual and progressive inspections performed under part 43 of this chapter.

| # | Cite | Requirement | Numeric threshold | Why it matters for major alterations |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | § 65.91(c)(1) | Currently effective mechanic certificate with **both** airframe and powerplant ratings, each currently effective | Each rating in effect **at least 3 years total** | Both ratings are required; an airframe-only or powerplant-only mechanic is not eligible regardless of experience |
| 2 | § 65.91(c)(2) | Actively engaged in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under the chapter | **2-year** period before application | Establishes current practical familiarity with Part 43 work, which is the framework a major alteration is approved under |
| 3 | § 65.91(c)(3) | Fixed base of operations, reachable in person or by telephone during a normal working week | — | Need not be where privileges are exercised, but must exist |
| 4 | § 65.91(c)(4) | Equipment, facilities, **and inspection data** available to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or related parts/appliances | — | Directly tied to Gate B: the IA must actually be able to lay hands on the approved technical data for the alteration |
| 5 | § 65.91(c)(5) | Pass a written test on ability to inspect per safety standards for returning aircraft to service **after major repairs and major alterations** and annual/progressive inspections under Part 43 | — | Major alterations are an explicit subject of the IA test, confirming the privilege is an IA privilege |

**Retest interval:** the sentence immediately following § 65.91(c)(5) provides that an applicant who fails the test may not apply for retesting until at least **90 days** after the date of failure.

---

## 3. Gate B — Privileges and limitations for major alterations, § 65.95

Verbatim operative text (eCFR current, fetched 2026-11-15):

> (a) The holder of an inspection authorization may—
> (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 [New] of this chapter, if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator; and
> (2) Perform an annual, or perform or supervise a progressive inspection according to §§ 43.13 and 43.15 of this chapter.

| Element of § 65.95(a)(1) | What the IA must be able to show |
|---|---|
| Scope of item | The item is an aircraft or related part or appliance — not limited to the airframe |
| Trigger | A **major repair or major alteration** has been performed (classification per Part 43 Appendix A) |
| Exclusion | Not an aircraft maintained under a **Part 121** continuous airworthiness program |
| Procedural basis | Approval made **in accordance with Part 43** |
| **Data condition** | The work **was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator** — this is the gating condition, not a formality |

**Administrative duties that condition exercise of the privilege (§ 65.95(b)–(c)):**
- (b) The holder must keep the authorization **available for inspection** by the aircraft owner, the mechanic submitting the aircraft/repair/alteration for approval (if any), and must present it on request of the Administrator, an authorized representative of the NTSB, or any Federal, State, or local law enforcement officer.
- (c) If the holder **changes fixed base of operation**, the holder may **not exercise the privileges** until the responsible Flight Standards office or International Field Office for the new base has been notified **in writing** of the change.

---

## 4. What is *not* a qualification — the errors this answer is designed to prevent

1. **A&P without IA cannot approve a major alteration for return to service.** The mechanic certificate is the *precondition* to IA eligibility (§ 65.91(c)(1)); it is not the authority to approve major alterations. The Part 43 text confirms the separation: approval requirements attach to persons authorized for the work, with an express carve-out that an Aircraft Maintenance Engineer may not approve a major repair or major alteration — and the IA privilege is separately conferred by § 65.95(a)(1).
2. **An IA cannot manufacture approved data.** § 65.95(a)(1) requires the work to have been done per *technical data approved by the Administrator*. If the alteration has no approved data (STC, FAA-approved data package, field approval), the IA cannot cure that by signing; the data approval is an FAA function.
3. **IA approval is not a design approval.** It is an inspection-and-return-to-service certification act.
4. **Part 121 continuous airworthiness aircraft are outside the privilege** (§ 65.95(a)(1)).
5. **Currency matters.** An IA whose fixed base changed without written notice (§ 65.95(c)) may not exercise the privileges, and an expired/unrenewed authorization carries no privilege at all.

---

## 5. Records that accompany an IA approval of a major alteration

From the fetched Part 43 text:

> (d) In addition to the entry required by paragraph (a) of this section, major repairs and major alterations shall be entered on a form, and the form disposed of, in the manner prescribed in appendix B, by the person performing the work.

> Appendix B to Part 43—Recording of Major Repairs and Major Alterations

Practical consequence: the **person performing the work** makes the major-repair/major-alteration form entry (FAA Form 337 per Appendix B) and disposes of it as Appendix B prescribes; the **IA** adds the approval for return to service. The IA's inspection is therefore not a substitute for the performer's Form 337 obligation — both exist.

Also from the fetched Part 43 text, on who may perform: a person working under the supervision of a holder of a mechanic or repairman certificate may perform the maintenance, preventive maintenance, and alterations the supervisor is authorized to perform, if the supervisor personally observes the work to the extent necessary and is readily available in person — **but that paragraph does not authorize any inspection required by Part 91 or Part 125, or any inspection performed after a major repair or alteration.** That last clause is the textual reason the IA (or other properly authorized approver) is needed at the end of a major alteration.

---

## 6. Operating checklist an IA should run before approving a major alteration

1. **Classify** the work: major alteration per Part 43 Appendix A (airframe / powerplant / propeller / appliance lists), or not listed in the aircraft specifications issued by the FAA → major. Record the classification basis.
2. **Identify the approved data** and its approval basis (e.g., STC, FAA-approved data package, field approval). Confirm the data covers *this* make/model/serial and *this* alteration, and that any FAA field approval is actually issued — not merely applied for.
3. **Confirm the as-installed condition matches the approved data** (parts, materials, torques, clearances, weight and balance revision, operating limitations, placards, AFM/POH revisions if required).
4. **Confirm the performer's entries** are complete (§ 43.9-type description and the Appendix B form / FAA Form 337).
5. **Inspect** to the extent necessary to establish the work conforms and the item is airworthy.
6. **Approve for return to service** in accordance with Part 43, and make the approving entry.
7. **Keep the authorization available** (§ 65.95(b)); **confirm fixed-base notification** is current (§ 65.95(c)).

If step 2 fails, stop: the data condition in § 65.95(a)(1) is unmet and the IA has no privilege to approve.

---

## 7. Currency, expiration and renewal (flagged as secondary)

- Expiration is governed by **§ 65.92** and renewal by **§ 65.93**. The verbatim text of those two sections **was not retrieved** in this research pass, so no figures for authorization duration or renewal counts are asserted here.
- The FAA *Inspection Authorization Information Guide* (secondary source, fetched 2026-11-15) contains chapters titled "Expiration of an Inspection Authorization" and "Renewal of an Inspection Authorization" and states, in fragmentary form, "at least one annual inspection for each 90 days" during the relevant period, that "the same logic applies to major repairs and major alterations," and that the numbers of annual inspections, major repairs, and major alterations "cannot be mixed." These are quoted as **fragments of a secondary document**, not as regulatory text; confirm against the current § 65.93 before relying on them.

---

## 8. Scope notes, inferences, and unresolved items (disclosed, not hidden)

| Item | Status |
|---|---|
| § 65.91(c) five eligibility items; 90-day retest sentence | **Verified** — verbatim eCFR current text |
| § 65.95(a)(1), (b), (c) | **Verified** — verbatim eCFR current text |
| Part 43 Appendix A / Appendix B exist and govern major-alteration classification and recording | **Verified** — section headings in fetched Part 43 text |
| Part 43 "Approval requirements" paragraph (inferred **§ 43.3(e)**) and the Appendix B recording paragraph (inferred **§ 43.9(d)**) | **Text verified; subsection letters inferred** — the fetch stripped paragraph headers, so the letters are my inference from the text |
| § 43.7 (persons authorized to approve for return to service after alteration) | **Not retrieved** — cited only as the parallel Part 43 authority provision; no text quoted |
| § 65.85 / § 65.87 (airframe and powerplant rating privileges) | **Not retrieved** — the rating-scope argument is stated structurally, not quoted |
| § 65.92 / § 65.93 (duration and renewal) | **Not retrieved** — no figures asserted |
| Avionics/radio alterations | **Unverified.** Whether a given avionics alteration is major, and which rating/authorization covers the sign-off, is not established by the retrieved text. Confirm with the responsible Flight Standards office before approving |
| Part 121 vs Part 91 applicability | § 65.95(a)(1) exclusion for Part 121 continuous airworthiness is verified; the assumption that the aircraft is Part 91 is an assumption, not a finding |

**Conflicting figures check:** the eCFR current text and the GovInfo CFR 2025 PDF fragments are consistent where the GovInfo extraction is legible (e.g., "has been in effect for a total of at least" three years; "at least 90 days after the date he failed"). The GovInfo extraction is partially scrambled (column-order artifacts), so where legibility is in doubt I relied on the **eCFR current** text as the governing current edition. No numeric conflict was found between sources.

---

## 9. Sources

1. 14 CFR § 65.91 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/section-65.91 (fetched 2026-11-15T19:12Z)
2. 14 CFR § 65.95 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D/section-65.95 (fetched 2026-11-15T19:12Z)

# INSPECTION AUTHORIZATION QUALIFICATIONS AS THEY APPLY TO MAJOR ALTERATIONS
**Basis: 14 CFR (eCFR, current edition as fetched 2026-11-15). Audience: AMT / IA applicant.**

---

## 1. SHORT ANSWER

There is **no separate qualification, rating, or endorsement for major alterations.** A mechanic becomes qualified to inspect and approve major alterations by holding an **Inspection Authorization (IA)** issued under **14 CFR 65.91**. The major-alteration element enters the regulation at exactly four points, and those four points *are* the answer:

| # | Provision | What it says about major alterations |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **§65.91(c)(5)** | The IA written test must examine the applicant's ability to inspect "according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after **major repairs and major alterations** and annual and progressive inspections performed under part 43." Major-alteration competence is *examined*, not separately certificated. |
| 2 | **§65.91(c)(4)** | The applicant must have available "the equipment, facilities, and **inspection data** necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance." For a major alteration this is the resource gate: you cannot qualify to approve one without access to the approved technical data. |
| 3 | **§65.95(a)(1)** | The privilege itself: inspect and approve for return to service after a major repair or major alteration **only if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**, and **not** on aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program. |
| 4 | **§65.93(a)(2)** | Continuing qualification: renewal activity may be met by performing "at least **two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days**" the authorization was held. |

**Bottom line for the AMT:** qualify for the IA under §65.91(c)(1)–(5); the major-alteration authority then exists as a *conditional privilege* under §65.95(a)(1), not as a standalone qualification. The condition — Administrator-approved technical data — is the one that disqualifies most attempted approvals in practice.

---

## 2. THE FIVE ELIGIBILITY ELEMENTS — §65.91(c), VERBATIM STRUCTURE

§65.91(b): "An applicant who meets the requirements of this section is entitled to an inspection authorization." §65.91(a): application is made on a form and in a manner prescribed by the Administrator (FAA Form 8610-1, *Mechanic's Application for Inspection Authorization*).

**(c)(1) Certificate and ratings.** Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with **both** an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, **each** of which is currently effective and **has been in effect for a total of at least 3 years**.
- Note the "each of which" construction: it is 3 years for the airframe rating *and* 3 years for the powerplant rating, not 3 years combined.
- Both ratings must still be effective on the date of application.

**(c)(2) Recent active experience.** Have been **actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before the date he applies**, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with this chapter.
- "This chapter" = 14 CFR Chapter I. Experience on non-certificated aircraft does not count.

**(c)(3) Fixed base of operations.** Have a fixed base at which the applicant may be located **in person or by telephone during a normal working week**; it need not be the place where the authority is exercised.

**(c)(4) Equipment, facilities, and inspection data.** Have available the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance.
- **This is the major-alteration resource requirement.** To approve a major alteration you must be able to lay hands on the *approved technical data* for that alteration (see §5 below).

**(c)(5) Written test.** Pass a written test on the applicant's ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service **after major repairs and major alterations** and for annual and progressive inspections under Part 43.
- Failure bar: an applicant who fails may **not apply for retesting until at least 90 days after the date of failure**.

*Amendment history of §65.91 as fetched: Docket 1179, 27 FR 7973 (Aug. 10, 1962), as amended by Amdt. 65-5, 31 FR 3337 (Mar. 3, 1966); Amdt. 65-22, 42 FR 46279 (Sept. 15, 1977); Amdt. 65-30, 50 FR 15700 (Apr. 19, 1985). No later amendment appears in the current eCFR text.*

---

## 3. THE PRIVILEGE AND ITS THREE CONDITIONS — §65.95

**§65.95(a)(1)** — the holder of an IA may "inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance **(except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter)** after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43, **if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**."

Three conditions must all be satisfied before an IA signature is valid on a major alteration:

1. **Subject matter** — the article is an aircraft, or a related part or appliance, that has undergone a *major repair or major alteration* (classification per §1.1 / Part 43 Appendix A — see §5).
2. **Data** — the work was done in accordance with **technical data approved by the Administrator**. The IA does **not** approve data; the IA approves *work*. If the alteration's design data is not already approved (type design, STC, or FAA field approval), the IA has no privilege to approve it and must route the data approval to the FAA first.
3. **Exclusion** — not an aircraft maintained under a **Part 121** continuous airworthiness program. (The regulatory text as fetched names Part 121 only; do not extend the exclusion by analogy to Part 125/135 without checking §43.7 and the operator's program.)

**§65.95(a)(2)** — annual inspection, and perform or supervise a progressive inspection per §§43.13 and 43.15. (Not a major-alteration privilege, listed for completeness.)

**§65.95(b)** — the IA must keep the authorization available for inspection by the aircraft owner, the mechanic submitting the aircraft/repair/alteration for approval, and present it on request of the Administrator, NTSB, or any federal/state/local law enforcement officer.

**§65.95(c)** — on **change of fixed base of operation**, the holder may **not exercise the privileges** until written notification is given to the responsible Flight Standards office (or International Field Office) for the new area. This is a self-executing suspension of privileges.

*Amendment history as fetched: Docket 1179, 27 FR 7973; Amdt. 65-2; 65-4; 65-5; 65-9; 65-35, 54 FR 39292; Amdt. 65-41, 66 FR 21066; Docket FAA-2018-0119, Amdt. 65-57A, 83 FR 9171 (Mar. 5, 2018).*

---

## 4. CONTINUING QUALIFICATION — §65.93 RENEWAL

An IA is valid for a **2-year period**. Renewal is not automatic; it is an evidence-based re-qualification.

**§65.93(a)** — during **March of each odd-numbered year**, at the responsible Flight Standards office, the applicant must present evidence that he/she **still meets §65.91(c)(1) through (4)** (note: (c)(5), the test, is not re-taken for renewal), **and** must show completion of **one** activity from (a)(1)–(5) **by March 31 of the first year** of the 2-year period **and one** activity **during the second year**.

The five qualifying activities:
1. At least **one annual inspection for each 90 days** the current authority was held; or
2. At least **two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days** the current authority was held; or
3. Performed or supervised and approved at least one progressive inspection per Administrator-prescribed standards; or
4. Attended and successfully completed a refresher course acceptable to the Administrator of **not less than 8 hours** of instruction; or
5. (Fifth activity — the oral-test alternative; see the discrepancy note in §7.3.)

**Do not mix categories.** The FAA's IA information guide states plainly that the counts of annual inspections, major repairs, and major alterations **cannot be mixed** to satisfy a single activity requirement. Pick one activity and satisfy it with that activity alone, in each year.

**§65.93(c) — loss and restoration.** A holder who does not complete one of the (a)(1)–(5) activities by March 31 of the first year **may not exercise IA privileges after that March 31**. Privileges may resume only after **passing an oral test from an FAA inspector** to determine that knowledge of applicable regulations and standards is current; passing that oral test is deemed to satisfy (a)(1)–(5) for the first year.

**§65.93(d)** — a person qualifying for relief under §61.40 may renew an expired IA under this section if §61.40 is met.

---

## 5. WHAT "MAJOR ALTERATION" MEANS — §1.1, AND WHY CLASSIFICATION IS THE FIRST STEP

**14 CFR §1.1:**
> *Major alteration* means an alteration **not listed in the aircraft, aircraft engine, or propeller specifications**—
> (1) That might **appreciably affect** weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other qualities affecting airworthiness; or
> (2) That is **not done according to accepted practices or cannot be done by elementary operations**.

> *Minor alteration* means an alteration other than a major alteration.

**14 CFR §1.1 (major repair, for contrast):**
> *Major repair* means a repair: (1) That, **if improperly done**, might appreciably affect weight, balance, structural strength, performance, powerplant operation, flight characteristics, or other qualities affecting airworthiness; or (2) That is not done according to accepted practices and cannot be done by elementary operations.

**Operating rules that follow from the distinction:**
- **Threshold clause first.** If the change *is* listed in the aircraft, engine, or propeller specifications, it is not an alteration of the kind the definition reaches at all. The classification test only begins once the change falls outside the specifications.
- **Alteration ≠ repair.** Same airworthiness-effect yardstick, different object (change to the article vs. restoration of the article). The approval path and the record are parallel, but the classification must be made on the correct object — a change made *while* repairing is still an alteration if it changes the configuration.
- **Part 43 Appendix A** contains the enumerated lists of major alterations, major repairs, and preventive maintenance. Appendix A is where you look for a named example before reasoning from the general definition.
- **The ARAC "Clarification of Major/Minor Repairs or Alterations" working-group material** (FAA docket material, fetched) confirms that the classification of major vs. minor has been persistently ambiguous, that the regulatory definitions were written to cover only certain cases rather than to be exhaustive, and that "appreciably affect" is the unresolved hinge. **Practical consequence for an IA:** record the classification rationale at the time of approval. If the classification is later disputed, the contemporaneous rationale is the defense.

---

## 6. THE THREE-GATE MODEL — HOW THE QUALIFICATIONS ACTUALLY GET EXERCISED

A major alteration passes through three separate gates, held by three potentially different people. Conflating them is the most common error in IA study material.

**Gate 1 — PERFORMANCE (does not require an IA).**
The alteration must be accomplished under Part 43. §43.3 sets the performance rules for alterations; §43.13 sets the methods, techniques, and practices standard. The person performing the major alteration need not hold an IA. A mechanic within the privileges of §65.81, a repair station within its ratings, or the holder of an appropriate Part 121/125/135 program may perform it.

**Gate 2 — APPROVAL FOR RETURN TO SERVICE (IA path is §65.95(a)(1)).**
§43.7 governs who may approve an aircraft, airframe, engine, propeller, appliance, or component part for return to service after maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, or alteration. For a major alteration the approving person must be one of the enumerated categories; the IA is one such category, and the IA's authority is bounded exactly as set out in §3 above. Alternatives exist (the FAA, an FAA designee, a repair station under its ratings and operations specifications, a Part 121/125/135 certificate holder under its own program) — and §65.95(a)(1) expressly carves out Part 121 continuous-airworthiness aircraft from the IA's authority.

**Gate 3 — RECORDING.**
§43.9 requires the maintenance record entry. For a **major repair or major alteration**, the person performing the work executes **FAA Form 337, Major Repair and Alteration** (§43.9(d)), and **Part 43 Appendix B** governs the form's content and disposition. The IA's approving signature on the 337 is the airworthiness act. The IA need not have performed the alteration, but must have inspected it and determined that it conforms to the approved technical data.

**Sequence rule:** Gate 2 cannot be cleared before Gate 1 and the data condition are satisfied. An IA signature on a 337 for work done to unapproved data is not an approval; it is an unauthorized return to service.

---

## 7. SOURCE RECORD, CURRENCY, AND DISCREPANCIES

**7.1 Primary sources relied on (eCFR current edition, fetched 2026-11-15):**
- 14 CFR §65.91 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-E/section-65.91
- 14 CFR §65.93 — http://ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-E/section-65.93
- 14 CFR §65.95 — http://ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D/section-65.95
- 14 CFR §1.1 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-1/section-1.1
- FAA, *Inspection Authorization (IA) Information Guide* (faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/ia_info_guide.pdf) — used **only** for the propositions that a major alteration requires FAA-approved technical data (independently supported by the §65.95(a)(1) text) and that renewal activity counts cannot be mixed across categories.
- ARAC *Clarification of Major/Minor Repairs or Alterations* working-group technical report (faa.gov/media/32151) — used only for the historical/ambiguity background in §5.

**7.2 Currency statement.** §65.91 stands at Amdt. 65-30 (1985); §65.95 at Amdt. 65-57A (2018). Both texts as fetched carry no later amendment. Re-verify against eCFR at the point of use — this document states the rule as of the 2026-11-15 fetch.

**7.3 Discrepancies found in the fetched corpus — stated, not smoothed over:**
- **(a) Subpart placement.** The fetched URL paths show §65.91 and §65.93 under `subpart-E` but §65.95 under `subpart-D`. This is a URL-path artifact. §§65.91, 65.93, and 65.95 all sit in **Part 65, Subpart E (Inspection Authorization)**; the section numbers and the text govern, not the path. Cite by section number.
- **(b) §65.93(a)(5) is missing from the fetch.** The fetched text refers to "paragraphs (a)(1) through (5)" and to "§65.93(a)(1) through (5)" but reproduces only (1)–(4) before jumping to (b). The fifth activity — the oral-test alternative — is therefore **not** verified from this fetch and is marked as item 5 without quotation in §4. The fetched paragraph (b) is likewise truncated/mis-lettered. **Verify §65.93(a)(5) and (b) on eCFR before relying on them.**
- **(c) §1.1 fetch is partially truncated.** The rendered §1.1 page shows the *Major alteration* lead-in and the *Minor alteration* line but cuts the (1)/(2) subparagraphs. The (1)/(2) text used in §5 comes from the quoted passage of the same page (same URL, same fetch) and is consistent with the definition as it appears in Part 43 advisory material. No conflicting figure exists in the corpus.
- **(d) OCR damage in the IA Information Guide.** The PDF extraction is fragmentary (sentences interleaved). Only the two propositions in 7.1 are drawn from it, and both are independently corroborated by rule text.
- **(e) AC 43-210A** is referenced in the guide's table of contents but was **not** fetched. It is not treated as authority anywhere in this document.

**7.4 Provisions cited that were not in the fetched corpus.** §§43.3, 43.7, 43.9, 43.13, Part 43 Appendix A, and Part 43 Appendix B are cited from the regulation as generally known; their paragraph lettering (specifically §43.7's subdivision letters and §43.9(d)) should be confirmed on eCFR before being quoted in a compliance document. The substantive propositions — that Part 43 governs performance and recording of alterations, that §43.7 enumerates who may approve for return to service, that a Form 337 is required for a major alteration, and that Appendix A lists major alterations — are not in doubt.

---

## 8. COMMON MIS-READINGS — CORRECT THEM BEFORE THE CHECKRIDE

1. **"The IA approves the alteration design."** False. The IA approves the *work* for return to service. Design/data approval is a separate FAA act (type design change, STC, or field approval). §65.95(a)(1) conditions the IA's privilege on data *already* approved by the Administrator.
2. **"The IA can approve major alterations on anything."** False. Part 121 continuous-airworthiness aircraft are expressly excluded by §65.95(a)(1).
3. **"A major alteration requires an IA to perform it."** False. Performance (Gate 1) and approval (Gate 2) are different acts by potentially different people.
4. **"The IA has airframe/rotorcraft/weight-class ratings."** False. The IA is a single authorization with no sub-ratings in Part 65. The mechanic certificate's airframe and powerplant ratings are the qualification basis (§65.91(c)(1)); scope of competence is a professional judgment, and §65.81 limits a mechanic's privileges to work within the ratings held.
5. **"Renewal is automatic if I keep my A&P."** False. §65.93(a) requires evidence of (c)(1)–(4) plus a qualifying activity in each year of the 2-year period; §65.93(c) suspends privileges for non-compliance.
6. **"I can mix annuals, major alterations, and training to make the count."** False per the FAA IA guide — one activity category per year, satisfied within that category.
7. **"Passing the IA test once covers renewal."** False. The §65.91(c)(5) written test is an issuance requirement; renewal looks only to §65.91(c)(1)–(4).
8. **"Failing the IA test means I reapply next week."** False. §65.91(c) imposes a **90-day** bar before retesting.

---

## 9. TEN-MINUTE VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (for the reader applying this)

1. Open eCFR Title 14, Part 65, Subpart E. Confirm §65.91(c)(1)–(5) matches §2 above, and note the amendment line at the bottom of the section.
2. Confirm §65.95(a)(1) still contains both conditions — "in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator" and the Part 121 exclusion.
3. Open §65.93 and confirm the full list (a)(1)–(5), including the fifth activity not reproduced in the fetched text, and confirm the March-of-odd-numbered-years timing and the 2-year period.
4. Open Part 1 §1.1 and confirm the major alteration definition's threshold clause ("not listed in the aircraft, aircraft engine, or propeller specifications") and both subparagraphs.
5. Open Part 43: confirm Appendix A (major alterations list), Appendix B (Form 337 content/disposition), and the current paragraph letters in §§43.3, 43.7, and 43.9(d).
6. Record the eCFR "current as of" date on your working copy. Regulatory answers without a currency date are not compliance answers.

---

## 10. ONE-SENTENCE ANSWER FOR THE AMT

You qualify to inspect and approve major alterations by holding an Inspection Authorization obtained under **14 CFR 65.91(c)** — current A&P with each rating in effect at least 3 years, at least 2 years of active engagement maintaining certificated aircraft, a fixed base of operations, the equipment/facilities/**inspection data** to properly inspect, and a passing grade on the written test that specifically covers return to service after major repairs and major alterations — and you may then exercise that authority only under **§65.95(a)(1)**, i.e., only on work done to **technical data approved by the Administrator**, and not on aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program.

question: IA
answer:
# Inspection Authorization (IA) — Qualifications, With the Major-Alteration Element

Source of record: eCFR, Title 14, Chapter I, Subchapter D, Part 65, Subpart D (§§ 65.91, 65.93, 65.95), and Part 43 (§ 43.3 and Appendix A). Pages fetched 2026-11-15; the text below is the rule text as fetched, and the rule text governs over any summary of it.

## 1. Bottom line

There is no separate 'major alteration' qualification. A person qualifies for an IA once, under **14 CFR 65.91(c)**, and the resulting authorization carries the major-alteration approval privilege by operation of **14 CFR 65.95(a)(1)**. So the answer has two halves: (i) how you become an IA, and (ii) what conditions attach when you use the IA on a major alteration.

## 2. The eligibility rule — 14 CFR 65.91

Verbatim, 65.91(a)-(c) (omitting only the amendment history):

> (a) An application for an inspection authorization is made on a form and in a manner prescribed by the Administrator.
> (b) An applicant who meets the requirements of this section is entitled to an inspection authorization.
> (c) To be eligible for an inspection authorization, an applicant must—
> (1) Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each of which is currently effective and has been in effect for a total of at least 3 years;
> (2) Have been actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before the date he applies, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained in accordance with this chapter;
> (3) Have a fixed base of operations at which he may be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week but it need not be the place where he will exercise his inspection authority;
> (4) Have available to him the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance; and
> (5) Pass a written test on his ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations and annual and progressive inspections performed under part 43 of this chapter.
> An applicant who fails the test prescribed in paragraph (c)(5) of this section may not apply for retesting until at least 90 days after the date he failed the test.

### Qualification checklist (all six must be true; 65.91(c) has five numbered elements, and (a) adds the application form)

| # | Requirement | Cite | How it is evidenced |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Application on the form and in the manner the Administrator prescribes | 65.91(a) | FAA application (FAA Form 8610-1 in current practice) filed with the responsible Flight Standards office |
| 2 | Currently effective mechanic certificate, **both** airframe and powerplant ratings, each currently effective, and in effect a total of at least **3 years** | 65.91(c)(1) | Mechanic certificate; note 'total of at least 3 years', not 3 years on each rating |
| 3 | Actively engaged for at least the **2-year** period immediately before application in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under 14 CFR | 65.91(c)(2) | Employment/work records; the engagement must be in maintaining aircraft, not merely holding the certificate |
| 4 | A fixed base of operations, where reachable in person or by telephone in a normal working week (need not be where the authority is exercised) | 65.91(c)(3) | Stated base on the application |
| 5 | Equipment, facilities, and inspection data available to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or related parts/appliances | 65.91(c)(4) | Applicant's own statement/survey; this is the 'can you actually do the work' element |
| 6 | Pass the written test on inspecting to safety standards for return to service after **major repairs and major alterations** and annual and progressive inspections under Part 43 | 65.91(c)(5) | Test result; on failure, no retest for at least **90 days** |

Points of construction that matter in practice:
- 65.91(b) makes entitlement mandatory on a showing: if all of (c) is met, the applicant 'is entitled' to the authorization. There is no discretionary 'suitability' element in the rule text.
- No type rating, no college/formal school requirement, no minimum flight-hour requirement, and no separate 'major alteration' endorsement appears in 65.91. Anyone who tells you an IA needs a type rating or an alteration-specific endorsement is adding to the rule.
- The **only** place 'major alterations' appears in the qualification rule is 65.91(c)(5) — as subject matter of the written test, not as an extra prerequisite.

## 3. The major-alteration authority and its conditions — 14 CFR 65.95

> (a) The holder of an inspection authorization may—
> (1) Inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance (except any aircraft maintained in accordance with a continuous airworthiness program under part 121 of this chapter) after a major repair or major alteration to it in accordance with part 43 [New] of this chapter, **if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator**; and
> (2) Perform an annual, or perform or supervise a progressive inspection according to §§ 43.13 and 43.15 of this chapter.
> (b) When he exercises the privileges of an inspection authorization the holder shall keep it available for inspection by the aircraft owner, the mechanic submitting the aircraft, repair, or alteration for approval (if any), and shall present it upon the request of the Administrator or an authorized representative of the National Transportation Safety Board, or of any Federal, State, or local law enforcement officer.
> (c) If the holder of an inspection authorization changes his fixed base of operation, he may not exercise the privileges of the authorization until he has notified the responsible Flight Standards office or International Field Office for the area in which the new base is located, in writing, of the change.

So the three conditions on the major-alteration privilege are:
1. **Scope exclusion:** not for an aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program. (65.95(a)(1).)
2. **Approved data:** the alteration must have been done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator. If the work devates from approved data, the IA has no authority under this paragraph to approve it for return to service; that is a matter for the FAA (this consequence is my reading of the conditional clause, and it is the ordinary reading).
3. **Part 43 procedure:** the approval must be made 'in accordance with part 43'. Part 43 therefore governs the record and the return-to-service act, not just the definition.

Administrative conditions that ride along: carry the authorization and produce it on request (65.95(b)); written notice to the responsible Flight Standards office before exercising privileges at a new fixed base (65.95(c)).

## 4. What the IA is *for* — the Part 43 backdrop

Part 43 is what makes the IA necessary. 14 CFR 43.3 states:

> However, this paragraph does not authorize the performance of any inspection required by Part 91 or Part 125 of this chapter or any inspection performed after a major repair or alteration.

And the Subpart D page likewise limits ordinary mechanic privileges — a certificated mechanic may perform or supervise maintenance, preventive maintenance, or alteration, but the airframe-rating and powerplant-rating return-to-service privileges in §§ 65.85 and 65.87 are expressly 'excluding major repairs and major alterations'. That is the gap the IA fills.

Whether a given change is a *major* alteration is a separate determination made under **Part 43, Appendix A**, which begins:

> (1) *Airframe major alterations.* Alterations of the following parts and alterations of the following types, when not listed in the aircraft specifications issued by the FAA, are airframe major alterations: …

(Appendix A then continues with propeler and powerplant/appliance major alterations in the same structure.) Eligibility under 65.91 does not decide whether the work is major; Appendix A does. Do not conflate the two.

## 5. Keeping the authority — 14 CFR 65.93 (relevant because major alterations are themselves a currency activity)

> (a) Except as provided in paragraph (d) of this section, to be eligible for renewal of an inspection authorization for a 2-year period an applicant must present evidence during the month of March of each odd-numbered year, at the responsible Flight Standards office, that the applicant still meets the requirements of § 65.91(c)(1) through (4). In addition, during the time the applicant held the inspection authorization, the applicant must show completion of one of the activities in paragraphs (a)(1) through (5) of this section by March 31 of the first year of the 2-year inspection authorization period, and completion of one of the five activities during the second year of the 2-year period:
> (1) Performed at least one annual inspection for each 90 days that the applicant held the current authority; or
> (2) Performed at least two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days that the applicant held the current authority; or
> (3) Performed or supervised and approved at least one progressive inspection in accordance with standards prescribed by the Administrator; or
> (4) Attended and successfully completed a refressher course, acceptable to the Administrator, of not less than 8 hours of instruction; or …
> (b) The holder of an inspection authorization that has been in effect:
> (2) for less than 90 days before March 31 of an even-numbered year need not comply with paragraphs (a)(1) through (5) of this section for the first year of the 2-year inspection authorization period.
> (c) An inspection authorization holder who does not complete one of the activities set forth in § 65.93(a)(1) through (5) of this section by March 31 of the first year of the 2-year inspection authorization period may not exercise inspection authorization privileges after March 31 of the first year. The inspection authorization holder may resume exercising inspection authorization privileges after passing an oral test from an FAA inspector to determine that the applicant's knowledge of the applicable regulations and standards is current. …
> (d) A person who qualifies for the relief prescribed in § 61.40 of this chapter is eligible to renew an expired inspection authorization under this section, provided the requirements of § 61.40 of this chapter are met.

Key consequences for someone whose practice is major alterations: 65.93(a)(2) lets 'at least two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days' of holding the authority serve as the currency activity. The renewal period is **2 years**; the evidence window is **March of each odd-numbered year**; the first-year activity must be complete by **March 31**; missing it suspends the privilege after March 31 until an FAA oral test is passed (65.93(c)). The 8-hour refressher option in 65.93(a)(4) is an alternative to any of the work-based options, not a supplement.

**Disclosed rendering anomalies (not my corrections):**
- In the fetched 65.93, paragraph (b) appears with only subparagraph '(2)'; the '(1)' is absent from the eCFR display. I quote it as rendered and do not supply a missing text.
- 65.95(a)(1) carries the eCFR artifact '[New]' after 'part 43'.
- The 65.93 page as fetched did not carry its amendment history; the 65.91 history ends at Amdt. 65-30, 50 FR 15700 (Apr. 19, 1985), and the 65.95 history ends at Docket FAA-2018-0119, Amdt. 65-57A, 83 FR 9171 (Mar. 5, 2018).

## 6. Common misreadings — each is a falsifier for a wrong answer

| Wrong statement | Why it fails | Correct position |
|---|---|---|
| 'An IA needs an additional endorsement to approve major alterations.' | No such element in 65.91 or 65.95. | One IA; the privilege is in 65.95(a)(1). |
| 'The IA can approve any major alteration.' | 65.95(a)(1) is conditional. | Only if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator, and not on a Part 121 continuous-airworthiness aircraft. |
| 'The 3-year clock runs per rating.' | 65.91(c)(1) says 'a total of at least 3 years'. | A total of 3 years across the airframe and powerplant ratings, each currently effective. |
| 'The 2-year engagement can be anything in aviation.' | 65.91(c)(2). | Must be maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under 14 CFR. |
| 'Failing the test costs nothing.' | 65.91(c)(5) closing sentence. | No reapplication for **90 days**. |
| 'The IA is good forever once issued.' | 65.93. | **2-year** period; renewal evidence in March of odd-numbered years. |
| 'An IA decides whether an alteration is major.' | Major/not-major is a Part 43 Appendix A determination. | 65.91/65.95 assume the classification; Appendix A supplies it. |

## 7. How to re-verify this answer at eCFR (repeatable procedure)

1. Open `https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-65/subpart-D` and confirm the subpart still contains §§ 65.91, 65.93, 65.95.
2. Open `.../section-65.91` — read (c)(1) through (c)(5) and the undesignated 90-day sentence; check the amendment history tail. If the tail has moved past Amdt. 65-30 (1985), reread the changed paragraph rather than relying on this memo.
3. Open `.../section-65.95` — confirm the 'technical data approved by the Administrator' clause and the Part 121 parenthetical are still in (a)(1).
4. Open `.../section-65.93` — confirm the 2-year period, the March-of-odd-numbered-years window, and the five activity options (including 65.93(a)(2) major repairs/alterations).
5. Open `title-14/part-43/appendix-Appendix A to Part 43` — confirm the airframe/propeler/powerplant major-alteration lists are unchanged, and `section-43.3` for the 'does not authorize … any inspection performed after a major repair or alteration' sentence.
6. Record the fetch date in any work product. eCFR is a point-in-time snapshot of a continuously amended title.

## 8. Scope note — what this memo does *not* cover

- **The alteration-classification lists themselves** (Part 43 Appendix A item-by-item) are named here but not reproduced; a full determination needs the Appendix A text and the aircraft specifications.
- **The record/approval form for major alterations** (the Form 337 / Part 43 Appendix B material) was **not** in the pages fetched for this answer. I do not state its rule number or content; verify it directly in Part 43 before relying on it.
- **Non-regulatory guidance** (Advisory Circulars, FAA Order 8900.x, the IA knowledge-test question banks) may explain practice but does not override §§ 65.91/65.93/65.95, and none of it was in hand here.
- **The requester's own status** (whether they hold an A&P, how long, whether they are seeking initial issuance or renewal) is unknown. The memo gives both paths; apply the one that matches.

## 9. One-paragraph answer for the record

Under 14 CFR 65.91(c), an IA applicant must (1) hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with both airframe and powerplant ratings, each currently effective and in effect a total of at least 3 years; (2) have been actively engaged for at least the 2 years before application in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under 14 CFR; (3) have a fixed base of operations reachable in person or by telephone during a normal working week; (4) have the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or related parts or appliances; and (5) pass a written test on inspecting to safety standards for return to service after major repairs and major alterations and annual and progressive inspections under Part 43 — with a 90-day bar on retesting after failure. Major alterations enter the qualification only through that test content; the authority to act on them comes from 65.95(a)(1), which lets the IA inspect and approve for return to service after a major repair or major alteration (except on aircraft maintained under a Part 121 continuous airworthiness program) only if the work was done in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator, with the authorization carried and produced on request (65.95(b)) and written notice to the responsible Flight Standards office before exercising privileges at a new fixed base (65.95(c)). The authority is renewed on a 2-year cycle under 65.93, and performing at least two major repairs or major alterations for each 90 days of holding the authority is one of the acceptable currency activities.

question: IA
answer:
COMPLIANCE ANSWER — QUALIFICATIONS FOR AN INSPECTION AUTHORIZATION (IA) AS THEY APPLY TO MAJOR ALTERATIONS
Governing rule set: 14 CFR Part 65, Subpart E (§§ 65.91, 65.92, 65.93, 65.95), read with 14 CFR Part 43 (§§ 43.3, 43.7, 43.9(d), Appendix A, Appendix B). Primary source: eCFR current text (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-65/subpart-E).
Answer identifier (value): 14 CFR 65.91 (eligibility) + 14 CFR 65.95 (privileges for major alterations).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
0. SCOPE, ASSUMPTIONS, AND FUNCTION LIMITS
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Assumed (state if wrong, and the answer changes):
- US federal rule set, 14 CFR, current eCFR text; not another jurisdiction and not a superseded edition.
- "FAA-AMT" is read as the aviation maintenance technician (mechanic) certification context, i.e., the question is a Part 65 mechanic/IA question, not a Part 145 repair-station or Part 21 design-approval question.
- "Inspection authorization" means the authorization issued to a certificated mechanic under 14 CFR Part 65 Subpart E — not an operator's Required Inspection Item (RII) program and not a repair-station article inspection.
- "Qualifications" means regulatory eligibility (certificate/ratings, experience, facilities, test), not an employer's training or job-task qualification standard.
- The inspection in question is the airworthiness inspection and approval for return to service after a major alteration.

Explicitly outside my function as Compliance Engineer: legal opinions or enforcement defense; non-US airworthiness authorities; and any determination that a *specific* alteration on a *specific* aircraft is major — that is a data-matching exercise against Appendix A and the FAA specifications (see §6) and cannot be done from the question as asked.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. THE TWO QUESTIONS THAT MUST NOT BE MERGED
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Most wrong answers to this question come from answering the performer question when the approver question was asked. They are governed by different sections.

| Function | Governing rule | Who is authorized |
|---|---|---|
| PERFORM the major alteration | 14 CFR 43.3(b),(c),(e),(f); 65.81; 65.85; 65.87; Part 145 | Holder of a mechanic certificate (43.3(b)); holder of a repairman certificate (43.3(c)); repair station (43.3(e)); air carrier under Part 121/135 (43.3(f)). A person working under supervision may perform work the supervisor is authorized to perform (43.3(d)) — but 43.3(d) expressly does NOT authorize any inspection performed after a major repair or alteration. |
| APPROVE for return to service after a major alteration | 14 CFR 43.7; 65.95 | For the general (non-Part 121 CAMP) case, the holder of an inspection authorization (65.95(a)(1)); repair station under Part 145; air carrier under Part 121/135 per its approved program. A mechanic certificate alone (no IA) does not carry this approval authority for a major alteration. |

Key point, stated plainly: a certificated A&P may perform a major alteration, but a certificated A&P without an IA may not approve an aircraft or part for return to service after a major alteration. That approval authority is the IA privilege in § 65.95.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. IA ELIGIBILITY — THE FIVE QUALIFICATION ELEMENTS (§ 65.91(c))
--------------------------------------------------------------------
To be eligible for an inspection authorization, an applicant must satisfy ALL five. Each is a hard gate; there is no partial credit and no substitution between them.

| # | Requirement | Citation | Evidence an auditor/FSDO checks |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Hold a currently effective mechanic certificate with BOTH an airframe rating and a powerplant rating, each currently effective and in effect for a total of at least 3 years | § 65.91(c)(1) | Mechanic certificate number, issue date, both ratings shown, no suspension/revocation; 3-year clock runs on the ratings |
| 2 | Have been actively engaged, for at least the 2-year period before the application date, in maintaining aircraft certificated and maintained under 14 CFR | § 65.91(c)(2) | Employment/work records, logbook or employer letters covering the 24 months preceding application |
| 3 | Have a fixed base of operations at which the applicant can be located in person or by telephone during a normal working week — it need not be the place where the IA is exercised | § 65.91(c)(3) | Address/phone of record; a P.O. box with no reachable presence does not satisfy this |
| 4 | Have available the equipment, facilities, and inspection data necessary to properly inspect airframes, powerplants, propellers, or any related part or appliance | § 65.91(c)(4) | Tooling list, current maintenance/overhaul manuals, AD and type-certificate data subscriptions, inspection checklists |
| 5 | Pass a written test on ability to inspect according to safety standards for returning aircraft to service after major repairs and major alterations, and for annual and progressive inspections under Part 43 | § 65.91(c)(5) | IA knowledge-test result (FAA Form 8610-1 application; test administered per the FAA IA program) |

Notes that matter in practice:
- The 3-year and 2-year figures are DIFFERENT conditions on DIFFERENT things: 3 years is how long the airframe and powerplant ratings must have been in effect; 2 years is how long the applicant must have been actively engaged in maintaining aircraft immediately before applying. Do not interchange them.
- There is no separate "major alteration endorsement" on an IA. The major-alteration approval authority is inherent in the authorization itself, subject to the limits in § 65.95 and § 43.7.
- Application is made on the form and in the manner prescribed by the Administrator (§ 65.91(a)); meeting § 65.91(c) entitles the applicant to the authorization (§ 65.91(b)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. CONTINUING CONDITIONS — DURATION AND RENEWAL (§§ 65.92, 65.93)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
An IA is not a lifetime credential, and the eligibility conditions in § 65.91 do not expire on issuance day.

- Duration (§ 65.92): the authorization expires on March 31 of each odd-numbered year. The holder may exercise its privileges only while holding a currently effective mechanic certificate with both a currently effective airframe rating and a currently effective powerplant rating. The authorization ceases to be effective if it is surrendered, suspended, or revoked; if the holder no longer has a fixed base of operations; or if the holder no longer has the equipment, facilities, and inspection data required for issuance. A surrendered, suspended, or revoked authorization must be returned to the FAA.
- Renewal (§ 65.93): to renew for a 2-year period the applicant must present evidence, on or before March 31 of the first year of the renewal period, that the applicant is still qualified under § 65.91, and must satisfy the activity requirement of § 65.93(b). The FAA IA Information Guide (fetched) describes that activity requirement in terms of "at least one annual inspection for each 90 days" during the period the authorization was held, with major repairs and major alterations (and training) as parallel activity types, and states that the number of annual inspections, major repairs, and major alterations performed cannot be mixed to satisfy the count. Treat the guide as descriptive; the rule text at § 65.93(b) governs and should be read verbatim before relying on the exact activity counts or combinations.
- Compliance consequence: an IA whose § 65.91(c)(3) or (c)(4) conditions lapse (no fixed base, no inspection data) has no effective authorization, and any approval signed in that state is an unsupported approval.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. WHAT THE IA MAY APPROVE AFTER A MAJOR ALTERATION (§ 65.95)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The operative privilege, as stated in the FAA IA Information Guide quoting § 65.95: with the exception of aircraft maintained in accordance with a Continuous Airworthiness Maintenance Program under Part 121, an IA may inspect and approve for return to service any aircraft or related part or appliance after a major repair or major alteration.

Conditions attached to exercising that privilege (each must be met before signature):
1. Approved technical data. The major alteration must have been accomplished in accordance with technical data approved by the Administrator (§ 65.95(a)(1)). FAA Order 8300.16A states the same requirement: "A major alteration requires the use of FAA-approved technical data. Minor alterations and repairs do not need" that level of data. If the data package is not approved data, the IA cannot create approval by inspecting — the data must first be approved (field approval under Order 8300.16A / AC 43-210A, STC, or other approved-data route).
2. The IA must actually inspect the work. The privilege is to inspect and approve; it is not a records-only signature.
3. Recording. The approval must be recorded per § 43.9. In addition to the § 43.9(a) entry, § 43.9(d) requires that major repairs and major alterations be entered on a form, and the form disposed of, in the manner prescribed in Appendix B to Part 43, by the person performing the work. Appendix B is the FAA Form 337 (Major Repair and Alteration) mechanism; the form carries the description of the work, the approved data reference, and the approval-for-return-to-service signature. Confirm the current Appendix B submission timing and office when completing the form.
4. Part 121 CAMP carve-out. For aircraft maintained under a Continuous Airworthiness Maintenance Program under Part 121, the § 65.95 IA route described above does not apply; approval runs through the certificate holder's approved maintenance program and its authorized personnel.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. LIMITS ON THE IA PRIVILEGE (WHAT AN IA MAY NOT DO)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
- May not approve for return to service a major alteration performed without FAA-approved technical data.
- May not approve work the IA has not inspected, and may not delegate the approval signature.
- May not approve for return to service an aircraft maintained under a Part 121 CAMP on the basis of the § 65.95 major-alteration privilege.
- May not act while the authorization is ineffective (expired, surrendered, suspended, revoked, or with the fixed-base/equipment/data conditions lapsed).
- May not use the approval signature to substitute for a required design/data approval. Data approval and return-to-service approval are two separate acts and are frequently confused; Order 8300.16A exists precisely to separate them.
- A person working under supervision under § 43.3(d) may not perform any inspection performed after a major repair or alteration — the post-alteration inspection is not delegable to an unsupervised helper.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. THE THRESHOLD DETERMINATION — IS IT MAJOR? (Part 43 Appendix A)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The entire approval question turns on classification, and the classification is not the IA's to invent. Appendix A to Part 43 supplies the test: alterations of the listed parts and types, "when not listed in the aircraft specifications issued by the FAA," are airframe major alterations; parallel lists exist for powerplant, propeller, and appliance major alterations. Appendix A lists, among others, changes to the empty weight or empty balance that increase the maximum certificated weight or center of gravity limits, and changes to the basic design of fuel, oil, cooling, heating, cabin pressurization, electrical, hydraulic, de-icing, or exhaust systems, and changes to wings or fixed/movable control surfaces affecting flutter and vibration characteristics. Appliance major alterations include changes in the basic design of radio communication and navigation equipment approved under type certification or a TSO that affect frequency stability, noise level, sensitivity, selectivity, distortion, spurious radiation, AVC characteristics, or ability to meet environmental test conditions.
Procedure: match the alteration against the Appendix A category lists; then check the FAA aircraft/engine/propeller/appliance specifications — if the alteration is listed there, it is not major by that route. If it is in a listed category and not covered by the specifications, treat it as major until the data proves otherwise.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. PRE-SIGNATURE COMPLIANCE CHECKLIST (THE PROCEDURE AN IA OR QA REVIEWER RUNS)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Run in order; stop at the first failure.
1. Verify the IA is currently effective: mechanic certificate with both ratings current; authorization not expired/surrendered/suspended/revoked; fixed base and equipment/data conditions still met (§§ 65.92, 65.91(c)(3)-(4)).
2. Classify the alteration against Appendix A and the FAA specifications; record the classification basis in the work package (§ 43 Appendix A).
3. If not major, the IA major-alteration privilege is not the operative authority — route to the ordinary § 43.9 approval path.
4. If major, confirm the alteration was accomplished under FAA-approved technical data and record the data identifier (STC number, field approval, AC 43-210A package, etc.) (Order 8300.16A; § 65.95(a)(1)).
5. Confirm the performer was authorized under § 43.3 (mechanic, repairman, repair station, or air carrier) and, where supervised work was used, that no post-alteration inspection was performed by an unsupervised person (§ 43.3(d)).
6. Physically inspect the alteration against the approved data: conformity, workmanship, clearances, system function, weight and balance revision if affected.
7. Confirm affected inspections/tests are complete and any flight test required by the data has been accomplished.
8. Confirm weight and balance and equipment list revisions are made where the alteration affects them.
9. Confirm FAA Form 337 is executed (description, approved data, performer signature) and that the return-to-service approval block is signed by the IA (§ 43.9(d), Appendix B).
10. Confirm the § 43.9(a) maintenance record entry: description of work, date, name and certificate number of the approving person.
11. Confirm Form 337 disposition per Appendix B (owner copy plus submission to the FAA as Appendix B prescribes).
12. Confirm no Part 121 CAMP conflict — if the aircraft is maintained under a Part 121 CAMP, stop; the § 65.95 route does not apply.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
8. COMMON NON-COMPLIANCE FINDINGS (audit hotspots)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
- A&P signs the return-to-service block on a Form 337 for a major alteration with no IA. Unsupported approval.
- IA approves a major alteration supported only by manufacturer's service information or a DER memo that was never FAA-approved as alteration data. Data approval and return-to-service approval conflated.
- IA approval signed after the March 31 odd-year expiration or after the fixed-base/equipment condition lapsed.
- Alteration performed by a supervised non-certificated person, including the post-alteration inspection, contrary to § 43.3(d).
- Appendix A classification never documented; the shop treated a listed airframe or powerplant alteration as minor.
- Form 337 executed but no corresponding § 43.9(a) logbook entry, or vice versa.
- Weight and balance not revised where empty weight or empty balance changed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
9. IF THIS IS AN AMT TRAINING QUESTION (FAA-AMT CONTEXT)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The examinable core, in the order the handbooks present it:
- A mechanic certificate with airframe and powerplant ratings permits performance of major alterations but not approval for return to service after them.
- The inspection authorization is the credential that carries major-alteration approval authority for non-Part 121 CAMP aircraft.
- The five eligibility elements of § 65.91(c), the March 31 odd-year expiration, and the § 65.95 privilege with the Part 121 CAMP exception are the standard test points.
- The major/minor call comes from Appendix A to Part 43 plus the FAA specifications, and the approval is recorded on FAA Form 337.
